title: Who Looks Like a Leader
text:
By the middle of the twentieth century, many researchers had concluded that personality traits had little to do with leadership. Influential reviews, including one by Richard Mann in 1959, found only weak and inconsistent links between traits and who became a leader.

In 1986 Robert Lord, Christy De Vader and George Alliger went back to the studies Mann had reviewed and reanalyzed them with modern statistical methods that correct for small samples and measurement error. They focused on a specific question: which traits predict whether a person is perceived as a leader by others in a group?

The corrected results told a different story. Intelligence was strongly related to being seen as a leader. Masculinity and dominance were also related, though less strongly. Lord and his colleagues argued that people carry mental prototypes of what a leader looks like, and they tend to grant leadership to those who match the prototype.

The authors were careful to note what they had and had not measured. Their analysis was about who is seen as a leader, not who actually makes groups perform better.
lesson: Groups tend to pick leaders who fit their picture of a leader. Separate that picture from the question of who will actually lead well.
people: Robert Lord, Christy De Vader, George Alliger
source: Lord, R. G., De Vader, C. L., and Alliger, G. M. (1986). A meta-analysis of the relation between personality traits and leadership perceptions: An application of validity generalization procedures. Journal of Applied Psychology, 71(3), 402-410.
